svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Security Hub determines resource criticality for exposure prioritization, and why the inference path matters. AWS states that Security Hub adds resource criticality to exposure prioritization to help central security teams focus on the exposures that threaten their most business-critical resources. There are two paths by which a criticality value arrives. The explicit path is an automation rule that the customer writes, with AWS's own example being marking every compute resource in a specific account as Very High, and such a rule applies both to resources already in the inventory and to new resources as Security Hub discovers them, which means it does not go stale as a static list would and is the right default. The implicit path is inference: Security Hub also infers criticality from resource tags and resource names, with no configuration required, and it records which source determined the value. The feature is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost, is always on for all customers, and requires no new enablement, so the inference path is active for every customer whether or not anyone chose it. The consequence, which is the central point of the post, is that resource names and tags, chosen for human convenience and for cost allocation rather than as security signals, are now an input to how security findings are ranked. Two concrete failure directions follow and they are asymmetric. A critical system carrying a dull name, such as a payments database still called db-2 after a 2019 migration, is likely to be read as unremarkable so its exposures sink in the queue. A retired load test stack still tagged Environment equals production is likely to be read as important and consumes attention that belongs elsewhere. The under-ranking direction is the more dangerous because old systems with poor names are disproportionately likely to carry real risk. The mitigating design is the provenance field, since Security Hub records which source determined the value, so inferred values can be distinguished from values an automation rule set, and that field makes the audit tractable: the question is not whether criticality is correct across every resource, which nobody can answer, but which important systems are sitting on an inferred value, which is a filter. Criticality is surfaced as a column on the Resources page where it can be sorted, filtered and grouped, and on the Impact assessment tab of an exposure finding. On value, criticality supplies the half that severity scoring lacks, since a severity derived from a CVSS base score is environment-blind by definition while criticality describes what the vulnerability is attached to, so the two multiply rather than compete. On operations, an existing exposure backlog may have reordered itself without announcement beyond a new column, so anyone working it top-down is working a different list. Recommended actions are to open the Resources page sorted by criticality and read both the top and the bottom, to name the five most critical systems from memory and find them in that list, to filter on the provenance field to separate inferred values from rule-set ones, to write automation rules for the systems that genuinely matter since an explicit value survives future changes to how inference works, to check for retired resources still tagged as production, and to tell whoever works the exposure queue that the ordering changed and why.
svg.title: Two paths to a criticality value: one you chose, and one that was already running
svg.text: The names you gave your resources now rank your security findings.
Security Hub resource criticality — always on, no enablement, already reordering your queue.
Path 1 — EXPLICIT, you decided
An automation rule — “marking every compute
resource in a specific account as Very High”
“applies to resources already in your inventory
and to new resources as Security Hub discovers them”
No stale list. AWS got the default right here.
Path 2 — INFERRED, nobody decided
“infers criticality from resource tags and resource
names, with no configuration required”
“always on for all customers” · “no new enablement”
This is the path every resource you have not written a
rule for is on, right now.
Names are chosen for people. Tags are chosen for finance. Neither was a security signal until yesterday.
They encode team habits, migration history, and whatever the console suggested at three in the afternoon.
And the failure is asymmetric — the quiet direction is the dangerous one
payments DB, still called “db-2” since a 2019 migration → reads unremarkable → exposures SINK
retired load-test stack, tagged Environment=production → reads important → eats attention
genuinely critical resource, named for its function → reads important → works as intended
Old systems with bad names are disproportionately likely to be the ones carrying real risk.
The field that makes this auditable
“records which source determined the value”
So the question is not “is every criticality right”, which
nobody can answer. It is “which important systems are
It completes what severity cannot do
A CVSS base score is environment-blind by definition.
Severity = the vulnerability. Criticality = what it sits on.
They multiply. Neither alone is a work queue.
sitting on an inferred value” — and that is a filter.
The ten-minute check
Name your five most critical systems from memory. Open the Resources page, sort by criticality, and find them.
Any that sit low is the gap this feature just created in your queue. Then write a rule for them.
Your exposure backlog may have reordered itself overnight, with nothing announcing it beyond a new column.
Same pattern as the week: a signal configured for one purpose, promoted to an input for another, with no notice given.
